findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: External residential placements for children increased from 52 to 58 since April, driving £4.144m overspend with weekly fees up to £15,100.
findings.detail: Children's Services external residential placements have grown from 52 to 58 since April 2026, a 12% increase in two months. The service is projecting £20.173m expenditure, an overspend of £4.144m. Weekly fees range from £3,700 to £15,100 depending on needs and complexity, with an average weekly cost of £7,280. This reflects both increasing numbers and continued high complexity of need.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising placement costs signal either demographic pressure or case complexity that the council's preventative services are not managing; placements at £15,100 per week are material outlays; if the trend continues, this will become a significant budget pressure.
findings.figures: 52 to 58 placements (12% increase since April); £4.144m overspend; average weekly cost £7,280; range £3,700 to £15,100 per week
findings.quote: Since April, the number of placements has increased from 52 to 58. Residential placements continue to reflect high levels of complexity and cost, with weekly fees ranging from £3,700 to £15,100, depending on needs, staffing ratios and therapeutic input. The average weekly cost is £7,280.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Gateway Centres PFI contractual costs of £0.599m overspend, continuing structural pressure.
findings.detail: Gateway Centres are forecasting a £0.599m overspend driven by higher rent costs associated with PFI arrangements at Eccles, Walkden and Pendleton. These are contractually agreed costs that exceed the budget available. The council notes this will be reviewed within the medium-term financial plan but signals a known, structural cost pressure.
findings.matters: A PFI cost that structurally exceeds budget is a fixed obligation; this represents a known, recurring pressure that will need to be addressed through MTFP changes or service reconfiguration; it signals budget-setting issues that have not been resolved.
findings.figures: £0.599m overspend
findings.quote: Gateway centres are currently forecasting an overspend of £0.599m. This is primarily due to higher rent costs associated with the PFI arrangements at Eccles, Walkden and Pendleton. These contractually agreed costs exceed the budget available and continue to place pressure on the overall financial position.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Total approved reserve drawdown of £21.417m in Q1 to offset overspends, reducing financial resilience.
findings.detail: The council is drawing £21.417m from approved earmarked reserves at Quarter 1 to partially offset underlying overspends of £28.077m. Major drawdowns include £6m for Adult Social Care, £5.085m for Place services, and £7.316m for Corporate Services. This level of reserve consumption at the start of the financial year signals that base budgets are not sustainable and the council is trading capital (reserves) for revenue stability.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite; drawing £21.4m at Q1 to offset overspends means these funds are not available for genuine emergencies or unexpected pressures; if overspends persist, reserve depletion will accelerate and the council's financial flexibility will deteriorate rapidly.
findings.figures: £21.417m total reserve drawdown; £28.077m underlying overspend before reserves
findings.quote: The forecast position for the year end is an overspend of £6.660m with areas of significant pressure being offset by underspends in other areas.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Commercial Properties portfolio forecasting £3.017m shortfall, managed through Incentive Reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The Commercial Properties portfolio is forecasting a shortfall of £3.017m against budget. This is being offset by drawdown of the Incentive Reserve, which was established to support the council's commercial operating model through market fluctuations. This represents a material income pressure.
findings.matters: A shortfall in the commercial property income stream of £3m represents either deterioration in market conditions or underperformance of the council's commercial strategy; while currently managed via reserve, continued shortfalls would erode financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3.017m forecast shortfall; Incentive Reserve drawdown of £3.017m
findings.quote: A forecast shortfall within the commercial portfolio is being proactively managed through the approved use of the Incentive Reserve. This reserve was established to support the Council's commercial operating model through market fluctuations.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Unify Programme repatriation of Adult Social Care underway with service transfers completed and next phase planned for October 2026.
findings.detail: The council is bringing Adult Social Care services back under direct council management. Two major transfers have been completed: Aspire transferred on 1st April 2026 and Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust on 1st June 2026. The programme has moved to Phase 2 with the Northern Care Alliance Foundation Trust transfer planned for 1st October 2026. The council has approved a £10m reserve for the programme but notes that additional costs for systems, estates and corporate support may emerge.
findings.matters: Major operational change in progress with significant financial commitment; the full cost of repatriation may not yet be quantified; if transfers are problematic or service continuity is disrupted, additional costs will accrue; the scale and complexity of bringing three major providers' services in-house simultaneously represents execution risk.
findings.figures: £10m reserve approved for Unify programme; transfers completed April and June 2026; next transfer October 1st 2026
findings.quote: The Unify Programme continues to progress in line with the Council's plans to bring Adult Social Care services back under direct Council management. During Quarter 1, two key milestones were achieved with the successful transfer of services from Aspire on 1st April 2026 and from Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust (GMMH) on 1 st June 2026... the programme has now moved into Phase 2, focusing on preparations for the transfer of services currently delivered by the Northern Care Alliance Foundation Trust (NCA), which remains planned for 1 st October 2026.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: £1m Housing Services savings target at risk due to recent directorate transfer and leadership changes.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget included a £1m savings target for Housing Services. The service has only recently transferred from Corporate and Adults Directorates to Place and is currently undergoing leadership changes. The council states that achieving £1m savings will require service stabilisation and transformation, and given the current circumstances the service is not yet sufficiently embedded to deliver sustainable savings of this scale without risking performance.
findings.matters: A £1m savings plan that is not expected to be delivered by Q1 of the financial year signals poor budget control; if this saving does not materialise, the council faces an additional £1m pressure by year-end.
findings.figures: £1.000m savings target; demand pressure allocation £1.000m also needed to be retained
findings.quote: Delivery of the £1m savings target remains a key objective however, achieving this will require a period of service stabilisation and transformation. Housing Services has only recently transferred into the Place Directorate and is currently operating through a period of leadership changes.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Housing overspend of £3.583m driven by temporary accommodation costs not recoverable via Housing Benefit or Local Housing Allowance.
findings.detail: Housing Services, recently transferred to the Place Directorate, is forecasting £3.583m overspend (before £1.759m reserve use) driven specifically by 'Housing Benefit Subsidy Loss' — temporary accommodation costs that cannot be recovered through the Local Housing Allowance or Housing Benefit system. After approved reserves, this leaves £1.824m unresolved overspend.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is demand-driven; if demand continues to exceed LHA/HB rates, this is an unrecoverable cost the council must absorb; this is a direct signal of housing stress in the council's area and indicates the £1m savings target for housing will not be met.
findings.figures: £3.583m overspend before reserves; £1.759m reserve drawdown; £1.824m overspend after reserves
findings.quote: Housing services is currently forecasting an overspend of £3.583m, primarily driven by the cost of temporary accommodation not able to be fully recovered through Local Housing Allowance (LHA) or Housing Benefit.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Adult Social Care underlying pressure of £18.245m with forecast £12.239m after reserve use, but £5.8m of known pressures not yet included.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care Operations is forecasting £12.239m overspend after drawing £6m from a £10m earmarked reserve. The underlying variance before reserves is £18.245m. Critically, this forecast excludes the full-year impact of 2026/27 provider fee uplifts (estimated £5.8m) and the anticipated 2026/27 pay award (£0.8m), both held centrally pending finalisation. The true underlying pressure is therefore substantially larger than the reported figure.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is demand-led and non-negotiable; a £18.2m underlying overspend plus £6.6m of quantified pressures still to hit the budget suggests the council faces a structural £24m+ pressure in this area; the Unify repatriation programme may introduce additional unquantified costs.
findings.figures: £12.239m reported overspend after £6m reserve drawdown; £18.245m underlying variance; £5.8m fee uplift pressure not yet included; £0.8m pay award provision pending
findings.quote: The current forecast does not yet include the full-year impact of the 2026/27 provider fee uplifts associated with Foundation Living Wage and contractual inflationary increases, estimated at £5.8m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block overspend of £24.494m driven by rising SEND demand and complexity.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block is forecasting £140.362m expenditure against a budget of £115.868m, a £24.494m overspend in a £115.868m budget (21% overspend). The council notes that financial pressures are concentrated in the High Needs Block reflecting increasing demand and complexity of SEND services. While a High Needs Stability Grant offers opportunity to address historic deficit, the in-year overspend remains at risk.
findings.matters: High Needs spending is statutory and driven by demand the council cannot refuse; a 21% overspend in the block signals either a shortfall in the stability grant, underestimation of demand, or failure of cost-containment measures; the council's ability to resolve this through SEND reform is unproven.
findings.figures: £140.362m expenditure vs £115.868m budget = £24.494m overspend; High Needs Block is subset of larger £239.077m DSG
findings.quote: Forecast expenditure totals £140.362m against a budget of £115.868m, resulting in an expected in year overspend of £24.494m. Financial pressures continue to be concentrated within the High Needs Block, reflecting increasing demand and complexity of need across SEND services.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Full-year overspend of £6.660m forecast at Quarter 1, with significant pressures concentrated in statutory services.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a material revenue overspend for the full 2026/27 financial year based on Q1 performance. Major service areas are overspending, with total approved use of reserves of £21.417m being drawn down to partially offset the position. The underlying overspend before reserve use is £28.077m.
findings.matters: A full-year overspend of this magnitude at Q1, only two months into the year, signals structural budget pressures that will require action; sustained reliance on reserves is not sustainable and signals deteriorating financial resilience.
findings.figures: £6.660m overspend forecast; £28.077m underlying before £21.417m reserve drawdown
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Quarter 1 revenue budget monitoring report forecasts a £6.660m overspend for the financial year with significant pressures in key service areas.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Capital programme rephased by £11.752m (10.5%) into 2027/28, with only 12% of revised budget spent in Q1.
findings.detail: The revised 2026/27 capital programme forecast is £111.224m, down from the £122.976m baseline approved in February. The report explicitly rephases £11.752m into the following year, and Q1 expenditure of £13.137m represents only 12% of the full-year budget, suggesting slower-than-planned delivery across the programme.
findings.matters: Slower capital delivery delays the council's ability to generate benefits and revenue streams needed to service borrowing on invest-to-save schemes; it also signals delivery capability constraints that extend beyond housing into the broader capital portfolio.
findings.figures: £11.752m rephased; £13.137m Q1 actual spend; £111.224m revised forecast
findings.quote: At the end of Quarter 1 actual expenditure was £13.137m with a forecast expenditure by end of March 2027 of £111.224m, leading to rephasing of £11.752m into the 2027/28 capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Staffing risks flagged on Place directorate (81% of capital programme) due to retention and recruitment challenges.
findings.detail: The report explicitly identifies forward delivery risks for Salford's largest capital directorate, noting that programme delivery is threatened by 'specific risks associated with internal resource to support the delivery of the programme in terms of both staff retention and recruitment, as well as interdependencies on third parties.' The Place programme accounts for £90.431m of the £111.224m total.
findings.matters: Unable to recruit or retain staff managing a £90m capital programme directly impairs the council's ability to deliver planned schemes and generate expected revenue returns from invest-to-save investments, with knock-on effects on borrowing servicing and financial position.
findings.figures: Place programme £90.431m (81.3% of total capital); total capital programme £111.224m
findings.quote: There are specific risks associated with internal resource to support the delivery of the programme in terms of both staff retention and recruitment, as well as interdependencies on third parties.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Housing Strategy and Enabling programme reduced by £16.950m due to revised cashflow forecasts and pending contract finalisation.
findings.detail: The housing delivery programme, a significant part of Salford's capital investment, has been scaled back substantially. The report notes that this reduction reflects 'revised cashflows forecasts while main contract arrangements are finalised,' suggesting delays in securing or finalising contracts with suppliers for planned housing schemes.
findings.matters: Housing is a material capital investment area; the scale of the reduction and the reference to pending contract arrangements suggest delivery or supply chain challenges that could affect completion timelines and borrowing profile.
findings.figures: £16.950m reduction from Housing Strategy and Enabling programme
findings.quote: Following a detailed review of the housing delivery programme, a net reduction of £16.950m has been made. This reflects revised cashflow forecasts while main contract arrangements are finalised.

findings.headline: Children's Services funded with successive annual increases totalling £3.3m for 2026/27 despite £3.1m investment in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council invested an additional £3.1m in Children's Services in 2025/26 to manage demand pressures, yet expects financial pressures to continue into 2026/27. The 2026/27 budget allocates £2.2m for price growth and £1.019m for demand growth. Underlying drivers are sustained demand for placements, rising unit costs, and increasing complexity of need, with growing dependence on higher-cost independent fostering and residential placements.
findings.matters: Successive years of additional investment with no moderation signal a structural funding problem; this pattern indicates Children's Services budgets will require continued growth, constraining the council's ability to fund other services, reduce borrowing, or address other departmental needs.
findings.figures: £3.1m additional investment 2025/26; £2.2m price growth budgeted 2026/27; £1.019m demand growth budgeted 2026/27; independent fostering and residential placement costs rising
findings.quote: Financial pressures are expected to continue into 2026/27, driven by sustained demand for placements, rising unit costs, and increasing complexity of need. This is resulting in greater reliance on specialist and higher-cost provision.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care integration partner overspent by £7.8m, forcing council to approve £4.842m mid-year budget increase
findings.detail: Northern Care Alliance, the council's primary Adult Social Care delivery partner, overspent by £7.8m in 2025/26, which is shared with NHS GM under the integrated fund risk-share arrangement. The council approved a £4.842m budget increase at Q3 to fund its share of this overspend. The NCA attributed the overspend to unachieved savings and cost/volume increases in Homecare and Supported Living, indicating structural demand pressures the partnership cannot manage within budget.
findings.matters: The integrated fund structure exposes the council to uncontrolled cost growth it cannot influence directly; unachieved savings suggest these overspends will recur, requiring sustained additional budget allocation or service reduction.
findings.figures: £7.8m NCA total overspend; £4.842m council budget increase approved; cost pressures in Homecare and Supported Living as key drivers
findings.quote: The NCA as primary delivery partner of ASC in Salford overspent by c. £7.8m which has been shared with the NHS GM as part of the risk share in the Integrated Fund. The NCA has confirmed that the key drivers of the overspend are unachieved savings, package of care cost and volume increases, particularly in relation to Homecare and Supported Living.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £34.237m requires ongoing council funding despite 90% government grant
findings.detail: The council recorded a £14.393m in-year DSG deficit in 2025/26, bringing the cumulative deficit to £34.237m. The government's new High Needs Stability Grant (expected Autumn 2026) will clear 90% of this deficit, but the council must fund the remaining 10%, equivalent to approximately £3.4m, from its own resources. The deficit stems from uncontrolled EHCP growth, rising exclusion rates, and expanded post-16 cohorts despite investment in local specialist provision.
findings.matters: The council faces a material future liability of £3.4m that will require drawdown from General Fund reserves or future budget reductions, directly constraining financial flexibility during a period of other demand pressures.
findings.figures: £34.237m cumulative deficit; £14.393m 2025/26 in-year; 90% grant / 10% council responsibility; £1.686m DSG reserve used in year; £1.5m Safety Valve Grant received
findings.quote: The grant is designed to clear 90% of the deficit based on the cumulative DSG position at March 2026, with the local authority funding the remaining 10%.

findings.headline: Audit recovery plan extends to 2028/29, with three years of disclaimed or qualified opinions before a clean sign-off
findings.detail: The auditor has published a recovery trajectory: 2025/26 will receive a disclaimer, 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be qualified, and only 2028/29 will reach an unmodified opinion. This reflects the scale of rebuilding required on the group consolidation issues and indicates material underlying deficiencies in financial reporting capability.
findings.matters: A three-year path to clean audit assurance is unusual and raises questions about the quality of internal controls, the competence of the finance function, and whether the council can produce reliable financial information
findings.figures: Planned opinions: 2025/26 Disclaimer (deadline 30 Jan 2027), 2026/27 Qualified (deadline 30 Nov 2027), 2027/28 Qualified (deadline 30 Nov 2028), 2028/29 Unmodified (deadline 31 Jul 2029)
findings.quote: This will mean we will issue a disclaimer of opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements. If we are able to complete our rebuilding procedures in 2026/27, we would move to a 'Qualified' audit opinion before moving back to an unmodified opinion in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Care Quality Commission assessed the Council as 'Inadequate' across all nine adult social care quality statements in May 2026
findings.detail: The CQC published an assessment of how well the Council fulfils its duties under the Care Act (2014) covering nine quality statements; the Council failed all nine. The auditors have identified this as a risk of significant weakness in value for money arrangements, particularly around the Council's ability to monitor and assess risk and evaluate service performance.
findings.matters: An 'Inadequate' rating from the adult social care regulator indicates systemic service failure in a major cost area and typically triggers intervention; combined with audit disclaimers, it signals serious governance and financial control deficiencies
findings.figures: Nine quality statements, May 2026 publication
findings.quote: The Council was assessed as 'Inadequate' across each of the nine quality statements.

findings.headline: Auditors issued disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial statements due to unresolved group structure accounting issues
findings.detail: The council's auditors could not complete testing of transactions and balances, particularly the treatment of changes in the Council's group structure. Disclaimers were issued for both 2023/24 (by 28 February 2025 backstop) and 2024/25 (26 February 2025), meaning those financial statements have received no audit assurance.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on independently verified financial statements; disclaimers mean the council's accounts cannot be trusted, and the underlying accounting issues suggest control or complexity problems in the finance function
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued: 2023/24 by 28 Feb 2025, 2024/25 on 26 Feb 2025
findings.quote: As a result we issued a disclaimer of opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements on 26 February 2025

findings.paper_title: Salford City Council Auditors Annual Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: First-time group accounts and multiple new accounting standards creating audit complexity; additional fees to be confirmed
findings.detail: Salford is producing group accounts for the first time in several years and applying multiple accounting standards for the first time, including ISA 600 (group audits), IFRS 16 (leases), and new asset valuations. Additional audit fees beyond the base £395,968 are marked TBC.
findings.matters: First-time group accounting and complex new standards introduce execution risk; undetermined audit fees suggest scope uncertainty, and asset revaluations (including Manchester Airport shareholding) could produce material adjustments.
findings.figures: Base audit fee £395,968; additional fees TBC for group consolidation, ISA 600, IFRS 16 leases, and asset valuations
findings.quote: Additional fees in respect of the Council producing group accounts for the first time in a number of years. This covers testing of the relevant transactions and balances at the subsidiary level and testing of the group consolidation.

findings.paper_title: Salford City Council Auditors Annual Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap increased 77% year-on-year from £38.1m to £67.4m over three years
findings.detail: The updated Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecasts a £67.4m funding shortfall over 2025/26 to 2027/28, up sharply from £38.1m in the prior year MTFS. The auditors note the Council recognises the increasing difficulty of identifying further savings without impacting front-line services.
findings.matters: A rapidly deteriorating funding position signals reduced financial resilience and limited ability to absorb further pressures or maintain debt servicing without service cuts.
findings.figures: £67.4m forecast funding gap 2025/26–2027/28; prior year MTFS showed £38.1m gap; opening 2024/25 budget gap £12.4m plus £14.9m service pressures
findings.quote: The latest MTFS details estimated a funding gap over the life of the MTFS totaling £67.4m million over the 2025/26 to 2027/28 period. This had increased from £38.1m in the prior year MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Salford City Council Auditors Annual Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £4.3m overspend on temporary accommodation due to rising costs and limited DWP subsidy reclaim
findings.detail: The Resources and Transformation directorate overspent by £5.4m, of which £4.3m stems from rising temporary accommodation costs and Housing Benefit Subsidy loss limits. The Council bears the full cost inflation above what DWP will reclaim.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs reflect both homelessness demand and cost inflation; DWP subsidy caps are fixed, leaving the Council exposed to full price increases.
findings.figures: £4.3m of the £5.4m overspend in Resources and Transformation attributable to temporary accommodation and Housing Benefit Subsidy loss
findings.quote: There has also been a £5.4m overspend in the Resources and Transformation directorate, mainly due to the Housing Benefit Subsidy loss, this £4.3m relates to the rising cost of temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Salford City Council Auditors Annual Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £3.2m overspend in children's services driven by rising Special Educational Needs (SEND) transport costs and increasing demand
findings.detail: Children's services overspent by £3.2m primarily due to SEND pressures. Rising transport costs and the increasing number of Educational Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) created demand-driven spending the Council could not control.
findings.matters: SEND costs are highly demand-inelastic and growing; transport inflation and rising EHCPs are structural pressures unlikely to ease without service policy change.
findings.figures: £3.2m overspend in children's services; rising numbers of EHCPs; rising transport costs
findings.quote: there has been an overspend in children's services of £3.2m, mainly due to Special Educational Needs Access and Delivery (SEND) with rising transport costs and rising demand for SEND services

findings.paper_title: Salford City Council Auditors Annual Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: Auditors issued disclaimer of opinion on financial statements due to missing deadline to complete audit procedures
findings.detail: The auditors could not complete the audit procedures necessary to obtain sufficient evidence before the Council's statutory deadline for publishing accounts. They issued a disclaimer of opinion, meaning no assurance was provided on whether the financial statements are accurate.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the lender has no audit assurance that the Council's financial position is accurately stated, creating material uncertainty about the true financial condition.
findings.figures: Audit report issued 26 February 2026 with disclaimer on accounts for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Our audit report included a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report did not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance was provided.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 update Report for 2025-26 OSB v4
findings.headline: Net income from service investments has been revised upward from £1.00m to £18.5m (an 18-fold increase), with the original budget apparently containing no service investment income at all
findings.detail: Table 22 shows the original 2025-26 forecast for net income from commercial and service investments at £1.00m; the revised estimate is now £18.5m. A footnote notes that the original approved Treasury Management Strategy Statement 'did not include projected net income from service investments.' The council holds £166.6m in service and commercial investments (shareholdings £49.3m, capital loans £77.6m, other loans £39.7m). The document does not explain what has changed or what these additional investments are generating.
findings.matters: An 18-fold upward revision to an income forecast without explanation is a red flag. This could indicate either new reliance on commercial returns (increasing financial risk) or an overly optimistic forecast. Lenders care about sustainable, reliable income; unexplained forecast shifts suggest either poor forecasting discipline or a recent strategic shift to depend on investment returns.
findings.figures: Original forecast: £1.00m. Revised forecast: £18.5m. Service investment holdings: Shareholdings £49.3m, Capital loans £77.6m, Other loans £39.7m; total £166.6m.
findings.quote: *The original estimate in the approved 2025/26 TMSS did not include projected net income from service investments.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 update Report for 2025-26 OSB v4
findings.headline: Investment balances have fallen by £58m in nine months (from £106m to £48m), driving a £46.6m rise in internal borrowing; the council is now financing capital from its own reserves instead of external markets
findings.detail: The council held £106.2m in investments at 31 March 2025 and £48.2m at 31 December 2025. In the same period, internal borrowing (the portion of the capital financing requirement funded by the council's own cash rather than external loans) rose from £224.7m to £271.3m. The treasury report explains this as the use of investment balances in the short term to fund capital expenditure, and notes the forecast shows available investment declining to £54.0m by year-end.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion of cash reserves reduces the council's buffer against revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs. Internal borrowing is only sustainable as long as capital programmes are well-managed and revenues hold; it is not a long-term financing source.
findings.figures: Investments: £106.2m (31 March 2025) → £48.2m (31 December 2025) → £54.0m forecast (year-end). Internal borrowing: £224.7m → £271.3m. Drawdown of £58.1m in 9 months.
findings.quote: The Council held £48.2m of investments as at 31st December 2025 (£106.2m at 31 March 2025)... increases to the capital financing requirement leading to an increase in the level of internal borrowing.

findings.headline: Reserve contribution of only £41k planned for 2026/27 despite 4% rental income increase
findings.detail: On a gross budget of £16.989m, the HRA is contributing only £41k to general balances despite 4% rental income growth and service charge increases. The council explicitly states that reserves must be maintained for volatility and unforeseen circumstances, creating tension between stated risk and actual reserve build-up.
findings.matters: Minimal reserve growth given the council's own emphasis on HRA volatility suggests limited headroom for unexpected costs or income shocks, particularly concerning given 92% of the budget is committed to PFI payments.
findings.figures: Contribution to balances: £41k on £16.989m expenditure (0.24% of budget); general reserves at £9.526m
findings.quote: The 2026/27 estimate reflects gross HRA expenditure of £16.989m including a contribution to balances of £41k.

findings.headline: Fire safety compliance costs are consuming income improvements that would have strengthened reserves
findings.detail: The council identified that improved income from shops and ground rents would have contributed more strongly to balances, but this improvement was partially offset by increased repairs and maintenance costs required to meet fire safety regulations. This shows regulatory compliance is a material constraint on reserve growth.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs that consume available margin reduce financial flexibility and restrict the council's ability to build reserves despite revenue increases.
findings.figures: Balances improved from budgeted draw-down of £0.062m to actual contribution of £6k in 2025/26, but constrained by fire safety spending
findings.quote: This improvement has been partially offset by increased repairs and maintenance costs required to meet fire safety regulations, along with a lower release of provisions than originally forecast.

findings.headline: Sheltered housing service charges increasing 16.32% in 2026/27 to address cost-income imbalance
findings.detail: Service charges for sheltered housing are rising from £38.92 to £45.27 per week, a £6.35 weekly increase. The council explicitly notes that these revised charges address imbalances between expenditure and income at the local level, indicating that service costs for sheltered residents are rising faster than rental income.
findings.matters: A 16% annual charge increase to vulnerable residents risks affecting collection rates and financial sustainability; this shows a specific service line under material cost pressure that a lender would need to monitor.
findings.figures: Sheltered service charges rising from £38.92 to £45.27 per week (16.32% increase)

findings.headline: Housing through Derive model dominates invest-to-save portfolio: 69% in 2026/27, growing to 87% in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Housing strategy accounts for £21.690m of the £31.390m invest-to-save borrowing in 2026/27, growing to £66.063m of £76.163m in 2027/28. The council's entire revenue sustainability increasingly depends on a single programme—the Derive affordable housing model—delivering forecast income and savings.
findings.matters: Revenue budget health rests on housing scheme performance. If Derive underperforms, the impact is severe and immediate. A lender needs to understand this concentration of risk in a single delivery model.
findings.quote: The Council is driving delivery models to provide truly affordable housing in Salford notably through investment in Derive. This model is delivering an extensive new build housing programme.

findings.headline: Invest-to-save borrowing planned to increase 143%, from £31.4m in 2026/27 to £76.2m in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The capital pipeline for 2027/28 shows invest-to-save borrowing of £76.163m compared to £31.390m in 2026/27. This step-change represents a material escalation in the council's reliance on schemes generating forecast savings and revenues, with corresponding increase in revenue budget exposure to scheme underperformance.
findings.matters: The rapid escalation signals growing financial risk and dependency on uncertain scheme returns. For lenders, this trajectory matters because revenue problems could emerge within the planning horizon if assumptions prove optimistic.

findings.headline: Revenue budget is exposed to shortfalls in invest-to-save scheme returns.
findings.detail: The council plans £31.390m invest-to-save capital borrowing in 2026/27. The strategy explicitly acknowledges that if forecast savings and income are not achieved, the resulting capital financing costs (interest and Minimum Revenue Provision) fall directly to the revenue budget, reducing resources available for services.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand this direct revenue exposure; a lender needs to know the revenue budget is at risk if the council's assumptions about scheme returns prove optimistic.
findings.figures: £31.390m invest-to-save borrowing in 2026/27; represents 34% of the £91.211m total capital programme
findings.quote: If the 'invest to save' business cases do not provide the expected revenue cashflow, the additional interest and MRP costs will by default fall to the revenue budget.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve held at £20.4m with no disclosed assessment of adequacy against risk
findings.detail: The council is maintaining the General Fund Reserve at £20.4m across the three-year period. The paper states this level "sits within the risk assessed range determined by the Section 151 Officer" but does not disclose what that range is, what the assessed risks are, or how the council's financial position has changed since the last assessment. With a growing budget gap, escalating savings requirements, and heavy use of earmarked reserves, the adequacy of this level is unclear.
findings.matters: A general fund reserve of £20.4m for a net budget of ~£464m (2026/27) is ~4.4%, which is often cited as prudent. But if the council is also using £26m+ of earmarked reserves in year one, the effective liquidity position is weaker. A lender needs transparency on what risks the council is hedging against and whether the reserve is adequate given the current trajectory.
findings.figures: £20.4m General Fund Reserve maintained across three years; net budget 2026/27 ~£464m
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the General Fund Reserve is forecast to remain at £20.4m over the period, consistent with the position set out in the 2026/27 budget report. This level sits within the risk assessed range determined by the Section 151 Officer.

findings.headline: Savings requirements escalate from £8.348m in 2026/27 to £15.334m by 2028/29, with no detail on deliverability
findings.detail: The MTFP projects cumulative savings/efficiencies of £8.348m in 2026/27, rising to £11.039m in 2027/28 and £15.334m in 2028/29. These are itemised across directorates (e.g. "Commissioned Placements 0.500m", "Public Health Contracted Services 0.337m") but many are not quantified against a baseline of how much is actually available to cut. The paper does not detail which savings have been tested, are in flight, or are aspirational.
findings.matters: If the council cannot deliver savings on this trajectory, the budget gaps grow larger. A lender assesses financial sustainability by looking at whether a council can deliver the savings it is relying on. Vague or untested savings are a red flag. By 2028/29, the council is betting on £15.3m of annual savings with no evidence of delivery capacity or risk mitigation if they slip.

findings.headline: Four PFI contracts are facing escalating costs of £3m annually, with no end date or exit strategy
findings.detail: The council manages four Private Finance Initiative contracts (from 2005). Over 20 years to 2024/25, it has drawn down £15.6m from an earmarked reserve to meet pressures in the contracts. "More recently," the paper states, these contracts "have been facing increasing financial challenges, primarily driven by rising costs in key operational areas such as building maintenance, staffing, and utilities," with "inflationary pressures" now amounting to "£3m annually." The paper does not detail contract end dates, escalation clauses, or exit costs.
findings.matters: PFI contracts are long-term liabilities. If the council is already drawing £3m annually from reserves to service four contracts, and inflation continues, this burden will grow faster than general fund growth. A lender needs to know when these contracts expire and whether the council has a plan to manage or exit them without triggering further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £15.6m drawn down over 20 years; £3m annual cost for building maintenance, staffing, utilities
findings.quote: More recently these contracts have been facing increasing financial challenges, primarily driven by rising costs in key operational areas such as building maintenance, staffing, and utilities. Inflationary pressures have significantly impacted the cost of service delivery, particularly in energy and facilities management, which are core components of the PFI arrangements currently amounting to £3m annually.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand up 6.4% in a single year and no clear ceiling
findings.detail: Numbers of residents in temporary accommodation have increased to 852, a 6.4% increase since the start of the year. The paper notes this is "lower than seen in previous years" but also acknowledges that "the demand for temporary accommodation has increased due to the lack of affordable accommodation." The MTFP assumes only 10 additional households per month will need temporary accommodation, a modest forecast given the recent 6.4% surge. The cost is poorly absorbed by housing benefit subsidy, leaving the gap to fall on the general fund.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost, volatile service that is difficult to turn off. A 6.4% jump in a single year, combined with a housing shortage and the incoming Renters' Rights Act, suggests demand could accelerate further. If the MTFP's conservative forecast (10 households/month) proves low, the council faces unbudgeted pressure on an already-tight general fund.
findings.figures: 852 residents in temporary accommodation; 6.4% increase since start of year; assumes 10 additional households per month
findings.quote: Numbers of residents accessing temporary accommodation has increased to 852, a 6.4% increase since the start of the year... The demand for temporary accommodation has increased due to the lack of affordable accommodation.

findings.headline: Planned use of £26.292m of earmarked reserves in 2026/27 alone suggests the budget is not balanced from internal resources
findings.detail: The MTFP shows directorates drawing £26.292m from earmarked reserves in 2026/27 (Adults and Health alone: £11.425m; Children's: £6.918m; Place: £6.000m; Corporate Services: £1.949m). Reserves are a one-off resource; once used, they are gone. The paper acknowledges that "reserves are one off resources and do not remove the requirement to deliver recurrent savings," but the scale of drawdown in year one (before even larger deficits appear) indicates the council is front-loading costs that should be managed from recurring budget.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial resilience by looking at the size and composition of reserves relative to risk. Drawing over £26m in a single year to balance the budget signals that the underlying budget is weaker than the headline figure suggests. If this pace continues, the council risks depleting reserves entirely within three years.
findings.figures: £26.292m planned use of earmarked reserves in 2026/27; cumulative use across three years: £11.425m + £0.557m + £0.174m for Adults and Health alone
findings.quote: Planned use of earmarked reserves 11.425 6.918 6.000 1.949   -26.292 0.000

findings.headline: UNIFY programme will triple adult social care workforce and is described as a 'significant challenge' to governance and financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council is bringing previously outsourced adult social care services back under direct provision. This will increase the council's directly employed workforce by one-third (from 377 to an implied ~500 staff across the directorate). The paper states this "presents a significant challenge to workforce capacity, governance, operational resilience, and financial sustainability" and requires "leadership, management and operational priority over the next 12–18 months." The MTFP allocates £10m of non-recurrent reserves to support the repatriation in 2026/27, but notes that once services transfer, the MTFP will need to be revised to reflect "innovation and transformation." This reads as: the true cost is not yet known.
findings.matters: A one-third increase in directly employed headcount, combined with an incoming £8m overspend from the service being taken over, suggests execution risk is high. If the repatriation encounters delays, tribunal costs, or payroll issues, the council may need to draw on reserves again or defer other investment. The fact that the MTFP is built on a placeholder (reserves) rather than a known, costed operating model is a governance gap.
findings.figures: One-third increase in directly employed workforce; £10m non-recurrent reserve allocation in 2026/27
findings.quote: This transformation will result in a one-third increase in the Council's directly employed workforce, with many staff transferring under TUPE regulations. Managing this scale of change presents a significant challenge to workforce capacity, governance, operational resilience, and financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Adult social care contract overspend of £8m in 2025/26 on top of transformation risk
findings.detail: The NCA (Northern Care Alliance) has reported a forecast overspend of approximately £8m on the health and adult social care contract in 2025/26. This is a current-year problem sitting alongside the UNIFY transformation, which will bring this service back in-house over the next 12–18 months. The paper notes that "currently Council officers have limited oversight of the financial position of services within existing providers," meaning the council is entering a major insourcing with incomplete visibility of what it is taking on.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically 30–40% of a council's net budget. An £8m overspend signals cost control failure in a key contract, and the planned insourcing of a poorly understood service carries execution risk. If the repatriation slips or reveals further hidden costs, pressure on the general fund could be severe.
findings.figures: £8m forecast overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: For 2025/26 the NCA has reported to NHS GM and SCC a forecast overspend on the health and adult social care contract of c£8m.

findings.headline: Forecast budget gap of £18.537m by 2028/29 with no funded solution
findings.detail: The MTFP projects a balanced budget for 2026/27, then deficits of £15.078m in 2027/28 and £18.537m in 2028/29. The paper identifies this gap but does not articulate how it will be closed, only that further 'financial review, challenge and prioritisation' will be needed. This represents a structural imbalance that grows each year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can sustain services without further cuts to frontline provision or without exceeding prudent borrowing. A gap this size, growing annually and unresolved, is a material financial risk.
findings.quote: The updated MTFP reflects the Government's 2026/27 to 2028/29 three-year local government settlement and highlights a potential budget gap of approximately £19m by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Business rates income below baseline, triggering dependency on £4.3m government Safety Net payment with further uncertainty ahead
findings.detail: Section 3.12 explains the council receives a 'Safety Net payment for 2026/27, as business rates income is less than baseline funding level. Because the level of bad debt assumed in the local government settlement is lower than Salford's budgeted amount.' Sections 3.11 and 3.14 note uncertainty over technical adjustments pending regulations and a data collection exercise, with retrospective adjustments possible in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile and sensitive to economic cycles and appeals. Dependency on the Safety Net indicates the tax base is below government assumptions. Future economic weakness could eliminate safety net protection. The acknowledged uncertainties in technical adjustments create risk that 2026/27 numbers may be restated.
findings.figures: £4.292m (Safety Net payment)
findings.quote: 100% Safety Net payment for 2026/27, as business rates income is less than baseline funding level. Because the level of bad debt assumed in the local government settlement is lower than Salford's budgeted amount.

findings.headline: Demand pressures in social care forecast to double from £5.3m to £12m annually over three years
findings.detail: Table 7 shows demand pressures growing from £5.329m in 2026/27, rising to £8.563m (2027/28) and £11.980m (2028/29). Section 8.11 states 'Demand needs continue to place financial pressures on children's and adult's care services.' These are embedded in directorate plans but represent accelerating cost drivers in areas where the council has limited discretion to reduce activity.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led: councils cannot refuse eligible service users. Demand growing faster than funding creates recurring budget pressure and dependency on efficiency savings or reserve drawdowns to manage. The trend suggests the council will struggle to fund social care from stable resources.
findings.quote: Demand needs continue to place financial pressures on children's and adult's care services. Services are developing strategies to manage needs-led pressures through the Innovate Salford programmes.

findings.headline: Council holds a £29.2m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit now funded 90% by government but 10% responsibility remains
findings.detail: Table 9 shows the DSG Adjustment account at -£29.178m across the forecast period. Section 2.9 notes the settlement provides that government will fund '90% of the local authorities Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficits through a High Needs Stability Grant,' leaving the council responsible for 10% of this deficit. The deficit reflects high-needs special education costs exceeding budget.
findings.matters: A £29m DSG deficit, even with government support for 90%, signals structural demand pressures in special educational needs that the council cannot fund from current revenues. This is typically driven by rising prevalence of SEND and increasing cost per pupil, creating ongoing cost pressure.
findings.figures: £29.178m (DSG deficit), 90% government funded, 10% council responsibility
findings.quote: The final settlement set out details for funding Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) deficits. The government has set out plans to fund 90% of the local authorities Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficits through a High Needs Stability Grant.

findings.headline: Council plans to drawdown £26.3m of earmarked reserves in 2026/27 to fund ongoing service delivery
findings.detail: Table 8 shows planned use of earmarked reserves totalling £26.292m in 2026/27, with further drawdowns of £11.606m in 2027/28 and £10.136m in 2028/29. These are reserves set aside for specific risks including adult social care, children's services, and capital commitments. Annual drawdowns of this scale deplete the council's financial buffers.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a key indicator of financial stress to lenders. Material year-on-year drawdowns suggest the council cannot fund its services from current income and is consuming its accumulated reserves, reducing its ability to handle unexpected pressures or shocks.
findings.quote: Directorates have detailed in their MTFPs the need for the planned use of earmarked reserves to manage the financial position

findings.headline: Budget relies on £11m of non-recurrent resources that will not be available in future years
findings.detail: Section 9.3 states the budget 'includes use of non-recurrent external funding from GMCA of £4.230m (provisional) and £6.770m from the Collection Fund surplus.' Table 6 shows these drop to zero from 2027/28 onwards. This masks the underlying structural budget pressure.
findings.matters: Using one-off funding to balance ongoing operational expenditure is not sustainable. This approach suggests the core budget position is under strain and the council is stretching available one-time resources to avoid deeper cuts or further borrowing.
findings.figures: £4.230m (GMCA), £6.770m (collection fund surplus), totalling £11m
findings.quote: The budget includes use of non-recurrent external funding from GMCA of £4.230m (provisional) and £6.770m from the Collection Fund surplus.

findings.headline: Budget shows unresolved cumulative gaps of £33.6m in 2027/28 and 2028/29 with no identified funding sources
findings.detail: Table 8 records 'Remaining budget gap / -surplus' of £15.078m in 2027/28 and £18.537m in 2028/29. The document balances 2026/27 using one-off resources and reserve drawdowns but projects significant deficits in the forward years with no savings or income proposals identified to close them.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty about structural sustainability. Two-year forward funding gaps of this scale, unaddressed at budget-setting, signal that the council's medium-term financial plan is incomplete or that difficult cuts are deferred.
findings.quote: Remaining budget gap / -surplus 0.000 15.078 18.537

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand continues to rise despite prevention efforts; 791 households as of March 2025
findings.detail: Households in temporary accommodation increased from 689 to 791 between April 2024 and March 2025. Children in temporary accommodation rose from 964 to 1,146. Despite strong prevention work generating £1.4m in savings, the absolute numbers continue to grow, indicating persistent cost pressure and unmet housing demand.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a material and growing cost pressure for councils; rising numbers despite mitigation efforts signal sustained demand growth and budget pressure.
findings.figures: Households: 689 (April 2024) to 791 (March 2025); Families: 510 to 584; Children: 964 to 1,146; Prevention spend £242,500 generated £1,378,600 in temporary accommodation savings
findings.quote: Households in temporary accommodation 1.4.24 was 689, increased to 791 as of 5.3.25. Families in temporary accommodation in the period raised from 510 to 584 and children in this period raised from 964 to 1146.

findings.headline: Unify Programme poses widespread transformation risk affecting service delivery and statutory responsibilities
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a major transformation integrating employees, processes and systems from three different organisations. The paper flags this as a new corporate risk with potential for widespread and significant negative impact on service delivery and failure to meet statutory responsibilities if not effectively managed. Full risk assessment is currently being completed.
findings.matters: Large-scale transformation programmes affecting statutory service delivery carry material execution risk that could impair the council's ability to meet legal obligations and maintain service standards.
findings.figures: New risk proposed to Corporate Management Team; full risk assessment underway
findings.quote: if the programme is not effectively managed and delivered, then there is a risk that bringing in employees, processes, and systems from three different organisations, may lead to misalignment in values, working practices, and expectations. This could lead to a negative impact on delivery of the service and failure to meet statutory responsibilities. The nature and scale of impacts from this risk could be widespread and significant.

findings.headline: Significant uncertainty in local government funding threatens financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council faces material uncertainty regarding future funding due to pending business rate reform and the fair funding reset from 2026/27. Reserves adequacy is under ongoing review as part of budget setting, and the paper explicitly states the need to ensure the council remains resilient in the face of emerging pressures and uncertainty.
findings.matters: For a lender, funding uncertainty and the adequacy of reserves are critical to assessing the council's ability to service debt and meet future financial obligations.
findings.figures: Risk score 16 (high); balanced budget approved February 2025 with MTFS to 2027/28; target risk score 3 by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Uncertainty in Local Government Funding: There remains considerable uncertainty regarding future local government funding, including the timing and impact of business rate reform, reset, and the introduction of fair funding from 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 (Audit Accounts Committee 24 Sept 2025)
findings.headline: 110 information security incidents reported in 2024/25; data governance review planned for 2026
findings.detail: The council reported 110 information security incidents in 2024/25, of which only one triggered mandatory ICO reporting. A comprehensive information asset review is planned for early 2026 to assess what information is held and how it is managed.
findings.matters: High incident volumes indicate either poor controls or extensive discovery of control gaps. GDPR and data protection failures create regulatory risk and potential fines. An information asset review suggests the council may not currently know what data it holds.
findings.figures: 110 incidents in 2024/25, 1 reported to ICO; information asset review commencing early 2026
findings.quote: In the financial year 2024/25, 110 information security incidents were reported, of which only one met the threshold required to be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). A review of the council information governance assets has been identified as an area for improvement and an information asset review will commence in early 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 (Audit Accounts Committee 24 Sept 2025)
findings.headline: Local Government Ombudsman upheld 82% of complaints investigated in 2024/25
findings.detail: The ombudsman investigated 11 cases and upheld 9 of them (82%). While the council states it implemented recommendations in 100% of cases, the high upheld rate suggests systemic service delivery or governance issues.
findings.matters: A high upheld complaint rate indicates governance or service delivery failures. This could signal underlying control weaknesses or inability to manage stakeholder issues, which affects council reputation and potentially future creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 11 cases investigated, 9 upheld (82%), 100% of recommendations implemented
findings.quote: the LGSCO investigated 11 cases, of which 9 (82%) were upheld. In 100% of cases, the LGSCO was satisfied that the council had successfully implemented their recommendations.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 (Audit Accounts Committee 24 Sept 2025)
findings.headline: Legacy enterprise system reaches end of support in 2027; major iTrent replacement program required
findings.detail: The council is replacing a 2000-era SAP ERP system that is no longer supported after 2027. This affects HR, payroll, and finance across the organisation. Implementation planned for late 2026. The system is described as critical with multiple interfaces and dependencies.
findings.matters: A failed or delayed system replacement creates operational and financial risk. Cost overruns or delivery slippage could strain budgets. System implementation disruption could affect financial controls during transition.
findings.figures: System implemented 2000, end of support 2027, replacement implementation late 2026
findings.quote: The council is replacing its legacy SAP HR, payroll, and finance system (also referred to as an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system), which was implemented in 2000. The technology platform will no longer be supported after 2027. It is therefore a critical business system which must be capable of meeting the council's needs.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 (Audit Accounts Committee 24 Sept 2025)
findings.headline: Workforce capacity and capability explicitly identified as a key strategic risk
findings.detail: The council flags this as a risk requiring targeted interventions. Over one-third of the workforce lacked digital identity. Improvements underway include digital skills development, apprenticeship expansion, and leadership development across all levels.
findings.matters: Workforce risks affect service delivery, financial performance, and stability of finance leadership. If capacity is constrained, key finance and governance functions may be at risk.
findings.figures: Over one-third of workforce lacked digital identity; HR & OD-led interventions including digital skills and apprenticeship expansion in progress
findings.quote: Strategic risk monitoring has identified workforce capacity and capability as a key risk. HR & OD has led targeted interventions including digital skills development, apprenticeship expansion, development of the Step into Salford pathways into employment programme and improved workforce planning. Over a third of the workforce previously lacked a digital identity

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 (Audit Accounts Committee 24 Sept 2025)
findings.headline: External audit for 2023/24 financial year not completed, no audit opinion issued
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars did not complete the 2023/24 audit due to statutory deadline changes. The most recent completed audit is 2022/23 (received October 2024). This leaves a significant assurance gap on financial statements for the year ending 31 March 2024.
findings.matters: A lender needs external audit assurance on financial position and controls. An uncompleted audit removes independent verification of the council's financial statements and risk management.
findings.figures: 2023/24 audit not completed; 2022/23 audit completed October 2024 with unqualified opinion
findings.quote: No opinion was expressed on the financial statements for the year ending 31 March 2024 as External Audit did not complete their audit due to changes in statutory deadline relating to the publication of the financial statements, which left insufficient time to complete the audit

findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £30m, indicating slower capital programme delivery than planned
findings.detail: Capital expenditure was £280.4m against a revised forecast of £310.2m, a shortfall of £29.8m. While this underspend freed up cash for investment at higher rates, it may indicate challenges in delivering planned capital investments within the year.
findings.matters: Repeated underspends can indicate slippage in the capital programme, which affects the council's ability to deliver service improvements and maintain assets. For a lender, it raises questions about delivery capability.
findings.figures: £280.4m actual spending vs £310.2m revised forecast; £29.8m underspend
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure (including impact of IFRS 16) 310.2 280.4

findings.headline: Service and commercial investment income provides 7.8% of funding, creating dependency and concentration risk
findings.detail: The council generated £21.25m in investment income from commercial and service investments (shareholdings, capital loans, and other loans), representing 7.8% of its total settlement funding assessment. This income stream is material to the budget and relies on the performance of underlying investments totaling £166.6m (shareholdings £49.3m, capital loans £77.6m, other loans £39.7m).
findings.matters: At 7.8% of funding, loss of investment income would create budget pressure. A lender needs to understand whether the council is dependent on income from unreliable or poorly performing investments.
findings.figures: £21.25m investment income; 7.80% of SFA; total service investments £166.61m
findings.quote: Total net income from Commercial and Service investments £m 21.25... Proportion of Settlement Funding Assessment (SFA) including collection fund income % 7.80

findings.headline: IFRS 16 accounting adds £121.2m finance lease liabilities to balance sheet, increasing Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: Under IFRS 16, finance leases previously classified as operating leases must now be recorded on the council's balance sheet as liabilities. This added £121.2m in recognized finance lease obligations, increasing the overall Capital Financing Requirement. These leases represent commitments that must be funded through future revenue.
findings.matters: This represents a substantial previously off-balance-sheet liability now creating a medium-term funding pressure. The council must now recognize these as part of its debt burden for lenders assessing financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £121.229m finance lease liabilities, increase to CFR from IFRS 16 leases
findings.quote: Finance lease liabilities of £121.229m, under IFRS 16 leases that the council had entered into that were classified as operating leases had to be accounted for on the councils balance sheet, this increased the councils CFR.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 remeasurement increased PFI liabilities by £41.9m through inflationary adjustments on existing contracts
findings.detail: Under IFRS 16 accounting, existing PFI contracts are remeasured annually using inflationary rates applied to the contract terms. In 2024-25, this resulted in £41.9m increase in recorded PFI liabilities across five schemes: Pendleton PFI (£14.9m), PFI 3 (£9.8m), LIFT (£5.5m), PFI 2 (£7.2m), and PFI 4 (£4.5m). The accounts are still being finalized and may contain further adjustments.
findings.matters: The council is locked into long-term PFI contracts with indexed interest rates, making future liabilities harder to predict and more exposed to inflation. This is not new borrowing but represents a substantial hidden obligation that now appears on the balance sheet.
findings.figures: £41.887m total PFI remeasurement; Pendleton £14.925m, PFI 3 £9.755m, LIFT £5.549m, PFI 2 £7.177m, PFI 4 £4.462m
findings.quote: The increase in the balance sheet value of PFI obligations was £41.887m as set out in table 11, under IFRS 16 PFI liabilities are remeasured each year using the inflationary rate applied to the contract for the year.

findings.headline: Council holds £52m LOBO loans with call option dates and sets aside £25m to manage refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council has £188m in LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can propose higher rates on set dates, creating refinancing risk. £78m of these loans had call option dates during 2024-25, and the council proactively repaid £26m in early prepayment offers to reduce exposure. To mitigate future refinancing risk, the council maintains £25m in dedicated investments timed to mature around LOBO call dates.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create material refinancing risk if lenders exercise options to raise rates. The council's active management of this (prepayments, cash reserves) suggests it is alert to the risk, but the £52m remaining exposure remains material.
findings.figures: £52m LOBO loans with call dates, £188m total LOBO exposure, £26m early repayment, £25m mitigation reserve
findings.quote: At the 31 March 2025, the Authority had £52m LOBO loans with call dates in 2024/25... To help mitigate the risk of such event the council now sets aside £25m of investments with DMO that mature around the date a LOBO loan option could be called.

news_drafts.lead: A PFI cost that structurally exceeds budget is a fixed obligation; this represents a known, recurring pressure that will need to be addressed through MTFP changes or service reconfiguration; it signals budget-setting issues that have not been resolved.

news_drafts.lead: Reserves are finite; drawing £21.4m at Q1 to offset overspends means these funds are not available for genuine emergencies or unexpected pressures; if overspends persist, reserve depletion will accelerate and the council's financial flexibility will…
news_drafts.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 - Cabinet
